findings.element: movementOne() — the hero numeral #count and the .delta pill, from D.lastFour / D.priorFour in lately.html
findings.problem: D.lastFour = sum(F.weeks.slice(8)) includes week 12, which is the current, unfinished week (partial: true, v: 12, commencing 13 Jul against a stated reading instant of Thursday 16 July 2026 — four days old). D.priorFour = sum(F.weeks.slice(4, 8)) is four complete weeks. The hero therefore reads 31 and the pill reads '+5 on the four before' from a comparison of three whole weeks plus four days against four whole weeks. Complete weeks only: 19 against 26, a delta of −7. The sign of the headline is an artefact of the incomplete bucket, and the band-head prints the window as 'Last four weeks · 22 Jun to 13 Jul', which runs three days past the reading instant. The surface's own shipping machinery refuses this: plan.html §01 quotes trend-series.ts:55 — buildTrendPoints 'skips any bucket not wholly inside the provider's covered window rather than zero-filling it'. Everywhere else on this screen the partial week is quarantined (hatched, labelled 'so far', spoken as 'so far'); the one place it is silently merged is the number the composition is built around.
findings.consequence: The owner asks the product's single question — am I getting on top of this or just busy — and is told, in the largest type on the screen, that she is five ahead of her normal. Like for like she is seven behind. The one figure she will quote to herself and to anyone else is not merely imprecise, it points the wrong way, and nothing on the surface lets her back the partial week out without summing three columns by eye.
findings.fix: Derive the comparison from complete weeks only. In the D accessor add `const whole = F.weeks.filter((w) => !w.partial);` and set `lastFour: sum(whole.slice(-4).map((w) => w.v))`, `priorFour: sum(whole.slice(-8, -4).map((w) => w.v))`; leave D.thisWeek as the partial figure. Change the band-head label to name the closed window it actually measures — `Last four whole weeks · ${whole.at(-4).start} to ${whole.at(-1).start}` — and print the current week beside the delta rather than inside it, as a second t-label reading `${D.thisWeek} so far this week, not counted`. If fewer than eight complete weeks exist, render the first-run treatment rather than a comparison. The chart still draws all twelve columns, hatched partial included.
findings.assertion: In every state, the hero numeral and the delta are computed only from fixture weeks whose `partial` is false: assert `hero === sum(weeks.filter(w => !w.partial).slice(-4))` and `delta === that − sum(weeks.filter(w => !w.partial).slice(-8, -4))`; with the shipping fixture assert hero 19 and delta −7. Assert additionally that the band-head window's end date is not later than the reading date, and that no week with `partial: true` contributes to either figure (flip the fixture's last week to `partial: false` and watch both assertions change).

findings.problem: `.record` is a zero-height element (`height: 0`, `border-top: 1px dashed`) carrying `animation: draw ... both`, whose `to` frame sets `clip-path: inset(0 0 0 0)`. A clip-path clips to the element's own border box — here 686×1px — and `.record-tag` is positioned at `top: -18px`, entirely outside it. Measured on the real file at 1440: `.record` computes `clip-path: inset(0px 0% 0px 0px)`, the tag's box is 103×15 at y 433 while the record box is 1px tall at y 450, and a pixel clip of the tag's own rectangle is a blank 206-byte PNG as built versus 1055 bytes with the clip forced off. This holds in settled, in `?motion=play`, on the dark ground, and under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` — the media query's `.record { clip-path: none }` is a normal declaration and is outranked by the animation's filled value, so the author's own escape hatch does not fire. 'Best week · 8' has never rendered, at any width, in any state.
findings.consequence: The chart draws a dashed horizontal line across it with no legend anywhere on the visible surface. The reader has to invent a meaning for it, and the obvious guesses — an average, a target — are not what it is. The line is the only thing on the screen that answers 'is this stretch better or worse than my normal', which is half the brief, and sighted readers never get told what it marks. Only the screen-reader sentence carries the fact.
findings.fix: Stop clipping. Change `@keyframes draw` to `from { opacity: 0; transform: scaleX(0); } to { opacity: 1; transform: scaleX(1); }`, add `transform-origin: 0 50%` to `.record`, and delete `clip-path` from both the `prefers-reduced-motion` and the `[data-motion="settled"]` blocks (keep `opacity: 1`). Because the tag must not be scaled with the line, move it out of `.record` and render it as a direct child of `.plot`: `Best week · ${D.bestPrior}` with `.record-tag { position: absolute; right: 0; }`, and give it the same 1.1s entrance delay so the reading order is unchanged.
findings.assertion: At 1440 and 390, on both grounds, in settled, in `?motion=play` after the choreography, and in a `reducedMotion: "reduce"` context, screenshot the record tag's bounding box and assert the clip differs from a screenshot of an equal-sized patch of flat card background — i.e. the words actually paint — and assert `getComputedStyle(document.querySelector('.record')).clipPath === 'none'`. Prove the assertion by restoring the clip-path and watching it fail.

findings.element: .bar-val ('12 so far'), .gridline b ('12' and '6'), and the last .colw, all right-anchored in .plot
findings.problem: Three pieces of chart furniture right-anchor into the same corner. Measured identically at 390, 768, 1280 and 1440 and on both grounds: `.bar-val` occupies 1204–1272 × 375–390 and the axis-top value '12' occupies 1246–1265 × 382–397 — a 19px × 8px overlap, i.e. the axis value is printed straight through the callout. The callout also overruns the plot's right edge by 7px at 1440 and 23px at 390, and sits 4px below the hero card's top border at desk widths (`.bar-val` resolves to `bottom: calc(100% + 6px)` on a full-height column, 21px above the plot). At 390 the '6' gridline value is additionally overprinted by the hatched column, which paints after the gridlines. A 3× capture of the hero reads '12 SO FA' with a grey '12' on top of it and the R clipped.
findings.consequence: The primary state of the master, at every width, carries garbled overprinted text on the hero card — the first object the eye lands on. Two of the three numbers involved are 12, so the reader cannot tell whether the chart tops out at 12, whether the week is at 12, or whether it is one number rendered twice.
findings.fix: Stop competing for the corner. Move the axis values to the left rail: `.gridline b { left: 0; right: auto; padding-left: 0; padding-right: var(--gap-hair); }`. Clamp the callout inside the plot for the final column: `.colw:last-child .bar-val { left: auto; right: 0; transform: none; }`. Reserve the callout's band in real layout instead of letting it overhang the card: add `margin-top: var(--gap-room)` to `.plot` and reduce its height to 144px so the hero card's geometry is unchanged.
findings.assertion: For every state that draws a chart, at 390/768/1280/1440 on both grounds: collect the bounding boxes of every text-bearing descendant of `.plot` (`.gridline b`, `.record-tag`, `.bar-val`) and assert no two of them intersect, and assert each one's box lies inside the `.hero` card's padding box. Prove it by restoring `.gridline b { right: 0 }` and watching it fail.

findings.element: every p, h1, h2 and h3 on the surface — no block-margin reset exists in the stylesheet
findings.problem: The file declares a named spacing ladder (4/8/12/16/24/32/48/72) and states that audit.mjs reads the SOURCE for raw px in margin, padding and gap so a token cannot drift from its value. There is no `p { margin: 0 }` (verified: no rule in the sheet sets a margin on a bare element selector), so every text block still carries the user agent's `em`-derived margins, which the source never writes and a source-reading audit therefore cannot see. Measured on the real file: h2.t-sect 21.58px top and bottom, h3.t-head 20px, h1.t-sect 17.42px, p.t-body 15px, p.t-small 13px, p.t-label 11px. Not one is a rung. Because these sit inside flex containers, they do not collapse — they add to the gap: the hero's figure block and its caption are separated by 37px (24px gap + 13px margin), and `.band-head` measures 89px tall for one line of heading and one label.
findings.consequence: The spacing system is nominal. Every vertical gap between text on the screen is a sum of a chosen rung and an unchosen number derived from a font size, so the composition's rhythm is neither the ladder nor consistent between roles — and the automated palette/ladder gate certifies it as clean because it reads the source, where those numbers do not appear.
findings.fix: Add `p, h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6 { margin: 0; }` to the reset beside `* { box-sizing: border-box }`, then restore the intended gaps explicitly with rungs: `.top-row` and `.band-head` already carry `gap`/`padding-bottom`; add `gap: var(--gap-tight)` to `.reading`'s wrapping and `gap: var(--gap-snug)` to `.fatal` (both already have it), and re-shoot every frame, because the whole page shortens.
findings.assertion: Across all seven states at 390 and 1440, assert every `p, h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6` computes marginTop and marginBottom of 0px; and separately assert that every non-zero computed margin, padding, row-gap and column-gap on every element on the surface is a member of {4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 72}. Prove it by deleting the reset and watching both fail.

findings.element: .bar.part, and interaction-check.mjs's 'the unfinished week is hatched, open-topped and says so'
findings.problem: The protected treatment is that the current week is hatched and open-topped because the week is not over, and the source comment repeats it. The rule writes `border: 1px solid var(--accent); border-bottom: 0;` — it opens the bottom edge, which sits on the baseline and is invisible, and closes the top with a 1px solid indigo stroke plus `border-radius: 4px 4px 0 0`. Measured: borderTopWidth 1px rgb(79,70,229), borderLeftWidth 1px, borderRightWidth 1px, borderBottomWidth 0px. The column renders as a fully outlined capsule — the shape that says 'finished'. The behaviour gate certifies the opposite by measuring the wrong edge: `open: parseFloat(cs.borderBottomWidth) === 0` is true of a column with a closed top and would stay true if the top stroke were made heavier.
findings.consequence: The one shape cue that distinguishes an unfinished week from a finished one is not in the pixels; the hatch and the 'so far' callout carry the whole load. And the surface's own regression gate reports the contract as proven, so this cannot be caught by re-running it — it would have shipped as a certified pass.
findings.fix: Open the edge that is actually visible: `.bar.part { border-left: 1px solid var(--accent); border-right: 1px solid var(--accent); border-top: 0; border-bottom: 0; border-radius: 0; }`, keeping the existing hatch background so the column reads as two verticals with the fill running out of the top. Then rewrite the gate's assertion to read the top edge.
findings.assertion: The current week's column computes borderTopWidth 0px, borderLeftWidth 1px and borderRightWidth 1px, and borderTopLeftRadius 0px, while every complete week's column computes a non-zero top radius and no border at all. Write the assertion against borderTopWidth first, observe it FAIL against the current build, then fix.

findings.element: .strip-scale in strip(), against the exactly positioned .dot and .fortnight
findings.problem: The dots and the fortnight line are positioned exactly (`left: calc(var(--x) * 1%)` from `age / D.axisMax`). The scale beneath them is not: `.strip-scale { display: flex; justify-content: space-between }` distributes four label boxes by their widths, so no label lands on the value it names. Measured centres against true positions: 'today' at 1.9% / 3.4% / 6.2% of the strip instead of 0% (1440 / 768 / 390 — a constant 19–20px error), '15d' at 34.7% / 35.8% / 37.9% instead of 33.3% (14px), '45d' at 98.9% / 98.0% / 96.3% instead of 100% (−11px). At 390 the '15d' label sits 21px right of the dashed fortnight line when the true gap between day 14 and day 15 is 7px. Worse, the marks are hard-coded `[0, 15, 30, 45]` while the axis maximum is derived — `D.axisMax = Math.max(45, Math.ceil((D.oldest + 4) / 5) * 5)`, with the comment 'A sixty-day job must not fall off the end of its own chart'. The fixture's oldest job is 41, which lands axisMax on exactly 45 and hides the error; at 42 days axisMax becomes 50 and every label is wrong by a further 10%, and at 56 days the label reading '45d' sits at the axis end, which is 60.
findings.consequence: The reader misreads how old her oldest work is — by two to three days at phone width today, and by up to fifteen days as soon as a job passes 41 days, which is exactly the reader this strip exists for. The fortnight threshold appears to sit at about twelve days, so the count above it stops being explained by the picture and starts contradicting it.
findings.fix: Position the scale the same way the marks are positioned. Replace the flex row with `.strip-scale { position: absolute; left: 0; right: 0; bottom: 0; height: 1.35em; } .strip-scale span { position: absolute; left: calc(var(--x) * 1%); transform: translateX(-50%); } .strip-scale span:first-child { transform: none; } .strip-scale span:last-child { transform: translateX(-100%); }` and render `const marks = [0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1].map((f) => Math.round(f * D.axisMax));` as `${n === 0 ? "today" : n + "d"}`.
findings.assertion: At 390/768/1280/1440, for every mark in the age scale, assert |labelCentre% − (labelDays / axisMax) × 100| ≤ 1 (and ≤ 3px). Run it a second time against a fixture whose oldest job is 56 days and assert the final mark reads '60d' and lands within 3px of the strip's right edge.

findings.element: kpi({ word }) in lately.html — the visible .t-small and the .sr accessible name
findings.problem: Each status card's phrase is written in the plural and paired with a count that can be 1. With the shipping fixture the third card renders '1' over 'have nobody's name on them' and speaks '1 job have nobody's name on them, of 9 jobs open'. The `plural()` helper is applied to the noun in the spoken name but never to the verb in the phrase, and never at all to the visible text.
findings.consequence: The product's voice is one of its stated arguments, and the surface prints a subject-verb disagreement in a card the owner reads every time. A screen-reader user hears it as a sentence, where it is worse. Any status count of 1 — the common case on a small venue's workspace — produces it, and three of the four cards can hit it.
findings.fix: Give each card both forms. Change the signature to `kpi({ n, one, many, glyph, i, unavailable })`, render `const phrase = n === 1 ? one : many;` into both the visible `.t-small` and the name (`${plural(n, "job", "jobs")} ${phrase}, of ${plural(D.open, "job", "jobs")} open`), and pass: sitting — one "hasn't moved in a fortnight", many "haven't moved in a fortnight"; overdue — one "is past the day it was due", many "are past the day they were due"; unowned — one "has nobody's name on it", many "have nobody's name on them"; waiting — one "is waiting on something else", many "are waiting on something else".
findings.assertion: Render the full state against a fixture where each of sitting, overdue, unowned and waiting is 1 in turn, and assert that every card whose numeral is 1 has visible text and an accessible name matching its declared singular phrase exactly, and that no card's name matches the plural phrase while its numeral is 1.

findings.element: #tip (position: fixed) and place() — no scroll handler on .scroll
findings.problem: The tip is placed once, in viewport coordinates, and never repositioned; the surface scrolls inside `.scroll`, not the document, so no scroll event reaches it. Measured with a mark focused by keyboard at 1440: the tip is placed at y 402 for a dot at y 474; scrolling the surface 260px leaves the tip at 402 while its dot moves to 734 — 268px of drift, still on screen, still naming a mark it no longer points at. Measured at 390 with touch: a tap pins the tip 8px above its dot; a 200px scroll leaves it 192px away, now below the dot. The source comment states that under touch 'the mark's title lives nowhere else on the screen, so this is the whole reading on a phone'.
findings.consequence: On a phone the reader taps a mark to find out which job it is, scrolls a little to see the rest of the strip, and the answer is now a floating panel sitting beside the wrong marks — the one place the job's title exists has become unanchored from the job. On the desk the same thing happens to a keyboard user, who has no pointer to re-establish the link.
findings.fix: Track the source. Keep the element the tip belongs to in a variable (`let anchor = null`, set in `show()` and cleared in `drop()`/`hide()`), and add `document.querySelector('.scroll').addEventListener('scroll', () => { if (!anchor || !tip.classList.contains('on')) return; const b = anchor.getBoundingClientRect(); if (b.bottom < 0 || b.top > window.innerHeight) { drop(); return; } place(anchor); }, { passive: true });`. Add the same handler on `window` scroll for safety.
findings.assertion: At 1440 with a mark focused by keyboard, and at 390 with a mark's tip pinned by touch: scroll the surface 200px and assert either the tip is dismissed, or the vertical distance between the tip's near edge and the mark's box is within 12px of what it was before the scroll. Prove it by removing the handler and watching it fail.

findings.element: .gridline b, .record-tag, .bar-val and .xaxis — none is aria-hidden; .xaxis span.mute uses opacity: 0
findings.problem: The chart carries a written equivalent in `.sr` ('Twelve weeks of finished work … 27 Apr, 5; 4 May, 3; … 13 Jul, 12 so far. The best week before this one was 8.'), and every piece of visual furniture is left in the accessibility tree beside it. Walking the chart's non-aria-hidden leaves returns, in order: '6', '12', 'Best week · 8', '12 so far', then all twelve x-axis dates — of which eight compute `opacity: 0`, because `.xaxis span.mute` hides them visually with opacity rather than visibility, which removes them from sight but not from the tree.
findings.consequence: A screen-reader user hears the twelve weeks as a sentence and then hears the same chart again as a stream of loose numbers and dates, including eight dates that are not on the screen at all. The reading the sr line was written to give is buried in the duplicate.
findings.fix: Hide the visual layer from assistive technology: add `aria-hidden="true"` to each `<span class="gridline">`, to `.record-tag`, to `.bar-val` and to the `<div class="xaxis">` wrapper; and change `.xaxis span.mute { opacity: 0 }` to `.xaxis span.mute { visibility: hidden }` so nothing invisible carries text at all.
findings.assertion: For every state that draws a chart, assert the accessible text of the `.chart` subtree is exactly the `.sr` sentence — no gridline value, record tag, bar callout or x-axis date appears outside it — and assert globally that no element with computed opacity 0 or width 0 contributes text to the accessibility tree.

findings.problem:
In the empty and error states, `
` contains no heading at all — the title is `

No work recorded yet

` and `

Tasks did not answer

`, styled at section rank but not marked as one, inside a `
` with no `aria-labelledby`. Measured: `main h1,h2,h3,h4` returns an empty list in both. Across all seven states, `[role=status], [aria-live], [role=alert]` returns zero elements. plan.html §07 specifies for the loading state 'a polite role="status" line'; what ships is `

Loading this reading.

` with no role, so it is inert text that is only found by walking to it.
findings.consequence: In the two states where something has gone wrong, a screen-reader user navigating by heading — the normal way to enter a page — finds 'Home' and then nothing, and no announcement ever tells them the reading failed or that it is being fetched. The error state is precisely the state where the reader most needs to be told what happened, and it is the state that says least.
findings.fix:
In VIEW.empty and VIEW.error, give the section an id and promote the title: `
` with `

No work recorded yet

` (and `mError` / 'Tasks did not answer' for the error state) — the `.t-sect` class already carries the type, so nothing changes visually once the block-margin reset above is in. Add `role="alert"` to the error card's `.center`. In VIEW.loading, change the line to `

Loading this reading.

`.
findings.assertion: Every one of the seven states renders at least one `h2` inside `main`, and each of those h2s is the target of its section's aria-labelledby. The loading state carries exactly one `[role=status]` and the error state exactly one `[role=alert]`; no other state carries either.

findings.element: LIMITS[1] in movementThree() — 'How a date moved'
findings.problem: Two things. LIMITS is a module constant and `movementThree()` takes no arguments, so the tile reads identically in all six rendering states — including `partial`, where the banner two movements above says 'Timeline did not answer this reading' and the coverage strip says 'Timeline did not answer'. plan.html §07 specifies for that state that 'the refusal slot for date movement changes its sentence to name the real cause. A reason that is wrong is worse than no reason.' It does not change. Second, the sentence reads 'The date recorder switched on in August.' with no year, on a surface whose reading instant is printed twice as 'Thursday 16 July 2026' — so a reader parses a past-tense sentence about a month that has not happened yet.
findings.consequence: In the reading where Timeline is down, the owner is given a cause that is not the cause: she will read that date history simply does not go back far enough, and will not learn that the source failed and that the answer may exist tomorrow. And in every reading she has to do arithmetic on an unanchored month to work out whether 'August' is behind her or ahead.
findings.fix: Make the refusals a function of the reading. Change the signature to `movementThree({ timelineAnswered = true } = {})`, pass `timelineAnswered: false` from VIEW.partial, and for the date-movement tile render `timelineAnswered ? "The date recorder switched on in August 2025; history accrues forward only." : "Timeline did not answer this reading, so no date history could be read at all."`. Anchor the year in the default sentence as written.
findings.assertion: In the partial state the date-movement refusal's text names Timeline and does not name the recorder; in every other state it names the recorder and does name a year. Assert globally that every month name printed anywhere on the surface is followed by a four-digit year.

findings.problem: Six places where the source no longer describes the file. (1) `.bar.live { background: var(--accent) }` — the live class is only applied when the last week is not partial, and the fixture's last week is always partial; `document.querySelectorAll('.bar.live').length` is 0 in every one of the seven states. (2) `@media (max-width: 900px) { .sk-row { grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr) } }` — no `.sk-row` element exists anywhere; it was left behind when the skeleton was rewritten to reuse the real components. (3) `.meter i.zero { background: var(--mark-ctx) }` — the class is applied when n is 0, but the same branch sets `--f: 0`, so the element is `scaleX(0)` and the colour can never paint. (4) The CSS comment 'Three gridlines, not a grid' and the JS comment 'Three gridlines with their values' both sit above `[0.5, 1].map(...)`, which draws two; the behaviour gate matches the code (`grid.n >= 2`) rather than the comment. (5) `@media (max-width: 560px) { .t-hero { font-size: 64px } }` restates the base value and changes nothing. (6) The first-run hero numeral has no `id="count"`, so the count-up entrance the comment calls 'the moment' runs in six states of seven.
findings.consequence: None of these is visible to the reader. They cost the next person who edits this file: every one of them reads as a live decision, and three of them describe behaviour that does not exist, which is how a fix gets aimed at the wrong rule.
findings.fix: Delete `.bar.live`, the `.sk-row` rule, `.meter i.zero` and the no-op `.t-hero` override. Correct both gridline comments to 'Two gridlines and the baseline' or render a third at 0.25 and leave them. Add `id="count"` to the first-run hero's `.t-hero` span so the count-up runs there too.
findings.assertion: Every class selector in the stylesheet matches at least one element in at least one of the seven states at at least one of the four viewports, and every declaration inside a media query changes at least one computed value relative to the same element outside it. Assert separately that `#count` exists in all six non-loading states.

findings.problem: `.page` contains `<header class="top">`, `<main>` and then `<div class="coverage">`. The coverage strip — which sources answered, which numbers the lab authored, when the reading was taken — belongs to no landmark, so it is skipped by landmark navigation and is not part of 'read the main content'.
findings.consequence: The surface's provenance apparatus, which is the thing that makes its honesty checkable, is the one region a screen-reader user is least likely to land on.
findings.fix: Wrap it: change `<div class="coverage t-label" data-type="label">` to `<footer class="coverage t-label" data-type="label" aria-label="What this reading was built from">` and close it as `</footer>`. No CSS changes — the class carries the layout.
findings.assertion: In every state, every element carrying visible text has an ancestor that is a `header`, `nav`, `main`, `footer`, `aside` or `[role]` landmark; assert specifically that `.coverage` resolves to a `footer` landmark with an accessible name.

biggestWin: Take the unfinished week out of the headline. The hero numeral and the '+5 on the four before' pill sum three whole weeks plus four days against four whole weeks; like for like the figure is 19 against 26, a delta of −7, so the one number the composition is built around currently points the wrong way. Everything else on this screen already quarantines the partial bucket — it is hatched, it is labelled 'so far', the shipping trend code refuses partial buckets outright — so this is a five-line change in the D accessor plus a re-worded band-head, not a redesign. It is also the only finding here that changes what the owner believes about her own business, and fixing it is what lets the rest of the surface's honesty apparatus mean anything.
